title: Give the name a place in the mind.
dek: In Chapter 9 of Positioning, Al Ries and Jack Trout treat the product name as a memory handle: a short verbal cue that helps an offer occupy a clear place in the prospect's mind. The right name makes the position easier to remember, repeat, and defend.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: A name is not a neutral label placed on a finished strategy. It can help a position enter memory, or make the offer harder to classify; choose the verbal handle with the prospect's mind in view.

canon.heading: Make the name carry the position.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 9, "The Power of the Name," from Al Ries and Jack Trout's Positioning on PDF pages 67-76. The chapter shows how a name can act as the hook that hangs a product on the prospect's mental ladder, while a vague or misplaced name leaves the position difficult to recall.
canon.readerIntro: Read this chapter as a naming and memory exercise. Mark how the authors distinguish descriptive, generic-like, negative, and confusing names; notice when a name makes the intended position easier to retrieve and when it narrows the future. Then write one naming and position brief for an offer you know. Stop at PDF page 76.

blocks.label: 01 / The name is a memory hook
paragraphs: The authors frame the name as the hook that hangs a brand on the product ladder in the prospect's mind. Naming therefore belongs inside positioning work, not at the end of it.
A useful name helps the prospect connect the offer to a category, benefit, or distinction quickly enough for the position to survive the noise of competing messages.

blocks.label: 02 / Choose for the prospect's associations
paragraphs: The relevant test is not what the name means to the people who invented the product. It is what the word causes the prospect to see, expect, and remember.
A name can make a product feel familiar and legible, or make it sound like an inside joke whose intended meaning never reaches the market.

blocks.label: 03 / Descriptive names can establish a foothold
paragraphs: A strong, almost-generic name can signal the territory an offer intends to occupy and make imitation harder for competitors to frame as the original.
The tradeoff is that a name closely tied to one position may constrain later expansion. That constraint is strategic only if the initial position is worth owning.

blocks.label: 04 / Confusion is a positioning cost
paragraphs: Names that are too technical, too common, or too similar to a larger competitor force the prospect to spend scarce attention figuring out what the offer is.
The no-name problem begins here: when the verbal handle does not create a distinct mental slot, the product has to fight to be remembered before it can be chosen.

blocks.label: 05 / Turn the name into a position brief
paragraphs: Choose a name by stating the category, the position it should cue, the associations it should invite, and the competitor or confusion it must avoid.
Stop with one brief that makes the name's intended mental work explicit. The test is whether someone can repeat the name and recover the position without a long explanation.

passageAnchors: the hook that hangs the brand
closeReading: What position does the name make easier to retrieve, and what does it make harder to imagine?
Which associations belong to the prospect rather than to the product team that chose the name?
When does a descriptive or generic-like name create a useful foothold, and when does it become a constraint?
Choose one offer: what competitor, category, or mental confusion must its name overcome?
Write a naming brief with the intended position, the associations to invite, the confusion to avoid, and the test for recall.

principle.heading: Make the name retrieve the position.
principle.body: A name earns its strategic role when it gives the prospect a short, distinctive path back to the position you want the offer to own.
principle.example: A team-inbox product that wants to own fast shared response could choose a name that cues a clear communication space rather than an internal technical architecture, then test whether prospects can explain its category and difference after one exposure.
principle.practice: Choose one offer and write three possible names. For each, state the position it cues, the association it creates, the confusion it risks, and the sentence a prospect should be able to repeat after hearing it once.

output.heading: Give the position a handle people can carry.
output.body: Choose the verbal cue that makes the offer easiest to place, remember, and repeat in the prospect's mind.

signals.heading: Four current signals on how names and promises become the interface for trust, discovery, and action.

fieldNotes.title: Hark names privacy as the route into the AI assistant category
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Hark released Hark Pro, an AI personal assistant positioned around using a computer end to end, while emphasizing privacy and task-related usefulness. The product exposes its web navigation to help users trust what the agent is doing.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: In a crowded assistant category, Hark is trying to make the name and promise do immediate classification work: private help that takes tasks off your plate. The positioning is less about abstract intelligence than a memorable relationship to the user's digital life.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether visible actions and the privacy promise create enough recall and trust to overcome the category's growing sameness.

fieldNotes.title: Meta expands the business assistant from answers to campaign action
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Meta said Ads Creative Studio is expanding to more advertisers and that its Meta AI business assistant is gaining deeper business context plus capabilities to plan, create, and optimize campaigns and schedule tasks and alerts.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The product is being named and framed as an operating partner for marketing work, not merely a chatbot. That clearer mental slot can reduce the explanation required before a marketer understands when to use it.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether the assistant's broader promise stays anchored to concrete campaign jobs, or becomes a vague label for a bundle of unrelated automation.

fieldNotes.title: Extreme weather turns a forecast into a merchandising constraint
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Retail Dive reported that the strongest Super El Niño on record is expected to disrupt weather patterns, complicating inventory and merchandising decisions as brands plan for a warmer winter and uneven cold snaps.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A broad external signal becomes useful only when translated into a specific decision frame: which seasonal promise will still feel true where the customer actually lives? Positioning has to meet lived conditions, not just calendar categories.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether retailers shift from generic seasonal language to locally legible needs, assortments, and messages as weather makes the old category cues less reliable.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI treats text provenance as a trust label
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI described its approach to text watermarking in response to EU AI Act requirements and explained a tool that can report whether it detects an OpenAI watermark without identifying the user or revealing prompts or conversations.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: Provenance is becoming part of the product's mental contract. A clear label can help people classify what they are reading and what the signal does, while an overbroad promise would create false certainty about origin.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether provenance cues become a useful shorthand for informed judgment, or are treated as a binary authenticity badge they cannot actually support.

tweets.author: Michael J. Miraflor
tweets.title: A product fragment on turning capability into behavior
tweets.summary: This fragment is useful because it names the behavioral question behind a new capability. The important test is not whether the feature is impressive, but whether it changes a repeated workflow enough for the user to adopt it.
tweets.text:
Hey friends, I need your wisdom. I’ll be reaching out to some of you individually, but this is an open call:

In about 3 weeks I’ll be presenting in front of ~50 professors of media, marketing, advertising, to give them some guidance / advice / inspo on how they should adjust their curricula and set their students up for success. I’m taking this opportunity super seriously because… AI.

I used to give this talk annually at CES, but this is the first time I’ll be doing it since ~2022, and so much has changed.

My ask: what advice would you give? Not to the students themselves but to those who are teaching and guiding them. Can be anything pithy, but if you’ve also written or tweeted etc about topic, I’d love to know.
